subtopics.title: US Military Strike and Justifications
subtopics.summary: United States forces carried out a military strike on Venezuela, known as Operation Absolute Resolve, which led to the capture of President Nicolas Maduro. Washington cited illegal migration, narcotics trafficking and alleged narco-terrorism, claims that Venezuela strongly contests. The action raised the question of whether a law enforcement objective can justify the use of military force on a sovereign territory.
facts: Operation Absolute Resolve: US military strike on Venezuela
Strike locations named: Caracas, Miranda, Aragua and La Guaira
The strike led to the capture of President Nicolas Maduro
US justifications: illegal migration, narcotics trafficking, alleged narco-terrorism
Venezuela rejects these claims and calls them a pretext for regime change
Washington designated Tren de Aragua and Cartel de los Soles as Foreign Terrorist Organisations
US alleges Cartel de los Soles operates under the leadership of Maduro
US alleges Cartel of the Suns collaborated with FARC to traffic cocaine into the US
Arguments in favour: fentanyl and narco-gangs cause mass American deaths
Arguments against: crime can become an excuse to violate borders

subtopics.title: Venezuela's Political and Economic Crisis
subtopics.summary: Venezuela has faced a deep political and economic collapse for several years, marked by hyperinflation, power outages, food shortages and a breakdown of healthcare services. The crisis escalated when Juan Guaido, Head of the National Assembly, declared himself Acting President, challenging Maduro's second term that began in January 2019. Nearly 8 million Venezuelans have fled the country since 2013, mainly to Latin American countries.
facts: Hyperinflation, prolonged power outages and food shortages cause severe humanitarian distress
Breakdown of healthcare services is part of the humanitarian crisis
Guaido declared himself Acting President, citing Articles 233 and 333 of the Venezuelan Constitution
Maduro was sworn in for a controversial second term in January 2019
The 2018 presidential elections were widely criticised as unfair and non-transparent
Opposition leaders were barred, imprisoned or exiled
The opposition-controlled National Assembly called Maduro a 'Usurper'
Economic contraction under Maduro is largely blamed on corruption, poor governance and overdependence on oil
Nearly 8 million Venezuelans have fled since 2013, mainly to Latin American countries
Currency: Venezuelan Bolivar; official language: Spanish

subtopics.title: US Sanctions and Strategic Interests
subtopics.summary: Washington imposed comprehensive sanctions on PDVSA, Venezuela's state-owned oil firm, to cut Maduro's access to oil revenue. Because sanctions failed to dislodge the government, the US turned to maritime interdictions aimed at choking oil revenues. Strategic interests include Venezuela's very large oil reserves and its partnerships with China, Russia, Iran and Cuba.
facts: US imposed comprehensive sanctions targeting PDVSA, the state-owned oil firm
Sanctions drastically limited Venezuela's oil exports to the US, forcing Caracas to seek alternative buyers
Maduro severed diplomatic ties with the US and expelled American diplomats
Venezuela has the world's largest proven crude oil reserves, estimated at over 300 billion barrels
Sanctions failed to dislodge the Maduro government, so the US turned to maritime interdictions
Venezuela's partnerships with China, Russia, Iran and Cuba cover energy, defence and finance
US views these alignments as a challenge to its strategic dominance in the Western Hemisphere
US revived Monroe Doctrine rhetoric, termed the 'Don-roe Doctrine'
Caribbean is treated as a critical zone of influence, reminiscent of Cold War-era calculations

subtopics.title: Monroe Doctrine and Limits of Multilateralism
subtopics.summary: The Monroe Doctrine, proclaimed in 1823, was initially defensive but later became a basis for US intervention in Latin America, expanded through the Roosevelt Corollary of 1904. The UN struggles to prevent unilateral interventions because of Security Council vetoes, unpaid dues and gray-zone tactics. Reform proposals include limiting P5 veto use and creating an accountability protocol for gray-zone threats.
facts: Monroe Doctrine: unilateral US foreign policy declaration proclaimed in 1823 by President James Monroe
Originally aimed to stop European powers from re-colonising Latin America
Roosevelt Corollary (1904) justified US intervention to maintain stability in the Western Hemisphere
Three core principles: non-colonisation, non-intervention, and US non-interference in Europe
P5 members (US, Russia, China, UK, France) can block any UN Security Council resolution
47 vetoes blocked 37 draft resolutions between 2015 and 2024
UN faces $2.4B in unpaid regular dues and a $2.7B peacekeeping shortfall
NATO, AU and ECOWAS intervene without UNSC approval
Modern gray-zone conflicts use cyberattacks, PMCs and proxies
Reform ideas: limit P5 veto use and introduce a veto override for mass atrocities

quizzes.passage: Venezuela has been at the centre of a sharp dispute with Washington. After Juan Guaido declared himself Acting President, tensions with Washington rose further. Caracas reacted sharply to these developments. The United States then imposed sanctions on the state-owned oil firm, which is central to the country's economy. Venezuela holds some of the largest oil reserves in the world, so the dispute has a strong energy dimension. Venezuela has also built relationships with several governments outside the region, and Washington has watched these ties closely. Caracas has rejected the allegations made against it, arguing that they are used to justify a change of government. Caracas also says that migration and drug issues are being used as a cover for political goals. Economic pressure has become a central feature of the dispute, shaping how both governments describe their goals and the steps they take next. Venezuela's economy has suffered deep problems in recent years, including high inflation and power outages. Shortages of food and problems in healthcare have added to the strain on ordinary citizens. Nicolas Maduro has led the government through these years, and critics have questioned the fairness of recent elections. Caracas and Washington give very different accounts of the dispute and its causes.

quizzes.passage: The Monroe Doctrine is one of the oldest foreign policy declarations of the United States. It was announced by an American president in the early nineteenth century, when European powers were looking to expand their presence in Latin America. The doctrine's early history is closely linked to the period after the Napoleonic wars. The policy rested on three core principles, which were set out when it was first proclaimed. Its first purpose was defensive, but the doctrine was later used to justify American intervention in the region. The Roosevelt Corollary of 1904 extended the doctrine, stating that the United States could act to keep stability in the Western Hemisphere. The United Nations was created to maintain international peace and security, yet it has very often struggled to stop unilateral military action by states. Some states have redefined the use of force as law enforcement or preventive self-defence. The Security Council is the body at the very centre of these efforts. Modern conflicts increasingly involve many hidden methods that blur the line between peace and war, and such conflicts are often described as gray-zone conflicts. Reform proposals have been put forward to make the Security Council more effective and more accountable.

quizzes.passage: The Monroe Doctrine is a policy that the United States announced in the early nineteenth century. It was meant to keep European powers from re-establishing colonies in Latin America, and the three core principles of the policy were stated at that time. Its first purpose was defensive, but later it was used to justify American military action in the region. The Roosevelt Corollary extended this idea, saying the United States could keep stability in the Western Hemisphere. The United Nations exists to maintain international peace and security, yet its work is often limited. Permanent members can block resolutions, and action frequently stalls when a major power is involved. The UN also faces funding problems, with unpaid dues and shortfalls for peacekeeping. Regional bodies have acted in crises without waiting for Security Council approval. Modern conflicts use hidden methods that blur the line between war and peace, and states have sometimes described military force as law enforcement. Reformers have suggested stronger accountability, limits on vetoes and public justification of decisions, and new rules for hybrid threats. Computer attacks, private contractors and proxies are among the tools used in these conflicts. Reform ideas also include a binding protocol for gray-zone threats and monitoring of cyber attacks.
